Guided wave testing for plant piping: screening, range and follow-up

Direct answer: Guided wave testing (GWT, also called GW, GWUT or long-range UT) sends low-frequency ultrasonic waves along the pipe wall from a ring of transducers clamped at one location, and records reflections from changes in cross-section such as welds, supports and corrosion. It screens long or hard-to-reach lengths of pipe quickly, but it is a screening tool: it does not measure remaining wall thickness. Any significant call-out needs follow-up with UT, corrosion mapping, profile radiography or another quantitative method before an inspector can use it in an API 570 corrosion-rate or remaining-life decision.

This section adds the practitioner detail that matters when GWT is used inside an in-service piping program: what the ASTM standards actually cover, what shortens range, how call-outs are followed up, and how the results fit the owner's API 570 obligations.

What the ASTM guided wave standards cover

Two ASTM practices describe GWT on above-ground steel piping. ASTM E2775 covers guided wave testing using piezoelectric transduction; ASTM E2929 covers magnetostrictive transduction. Their stated scopes are similar and are worth knowing, because they define the conditions under which the technique is on firm ground:

  • Material and size. Carbon steel or low-alloy steel pipe, NPS 2 to 48, with wall thickness between 0.15 and 1 inch (3.81 to 25.4 mm).
  • Basic configuration. Straight pipe of a single size and schedule, fully accessible at the test location, joined by girth welds, held on simple contact supports, and free of internal or external coatings. E2929 notes that insulation and paint are acceptable within its basic configuration.
  • Screening only. Both standards state that GWT is a screening tool and does not provide a direct measurement of wall thickness.
  • Follow-up expected. Where a possible defect is found, follow-up of the suspect area with UT or other NDT is normally required to obtain detailed thickness information.

The current active versions listed by ASTM are E2775-16 (reapproved 2023) and E2929-18 (reapproved 2022). The UK also publishes BS 9690 parts on guided wave testing. Owners can and do apply GWT outside the basic configuration (bends, coated lines, buried sections), but the procedure must then address those conditions explicitly, and the reliability of the screen falls as complexity rises.

Where GWT earns its place in an API 570 program

API 570 requires owners to inspect piping for the damage mechanisms that apply, with particular attention to locations where damage concentrates and that are hard to reach. GWT is most useful where conventional access is expensive or disruptive:

  • Insulated piping susceptible to CUI. A single collar location, with a small window of insulation removed, screens a length of insulated pipe in each direction. Call-outs show where to strip insulation for follow-up. See CUI inspection and the broader CUI monitoring guide.
  • Road crossings, casings and wall penetrations. Sections that cannot be reached without excavation or demolition.
  • Soil-to-air interfaces and short buried sections. Places where piping enters the ground and corrosion concentrates; range into soil is usually much shorter than in air.
  • Pipe racks and elevated runs. Long runs where scaffolding for spot UT would be costly.
  • Under supports. Contact-point corrosion at supports is a common screen target, though supports themselves generate reflections that the analyst must separate from damage.

GWT does not replace the CML program. It tells the inspector where to look; the CML readings and follow-up measurements are what feed the corrosion rate. For the circuit and CML framework, see piping circuit and CML inspection.

What limits range and sensitivity

Range quoted in sales literature is usually for clean, straight, uncoated pipe in air. Real plant piping rarely looks like that. The main factors that shorten range or blur the screen:

ConditionEffect on GWTPractical response
Bends and elbowsDistort the wave mode; reduce sensitivity beyond the bendAdd test locations on each side; treat beyond-bend results with caution
Heavy or bonded coatings (bitumen, wraps, some epoxies)Absorb energy; sharply reduce rangeShorter test spacing; consider other screening methods
Buried pipe and soil contactEnergy leaks into surrounding soilShorter range; excavate for test locations as needed
Flanges, valves, tees and branchesStrong reflections; little or no transmission past many fittingsTreat each as a test-section boundary
Clamped or welded supportsReflections that can mask or mimic corrosionMap supports in the field and compare with signals
Liquid contents and depositsCan attenuate some wave modesNote service conditions in the procedure
Small, isolated pits and gradual wall lossLow cross-section change; hard to detectRely on CMLs and scanning, not GWT, for these mechanisms
TemperatureEquipment and collar temperature limits applyConfirm limits with the system and procedure

The most important limitation is the last few rows: GWT responds to the loss of cross-sectional area around the circumference, so a small isolated pit can be invisible to it. That is why it is a poor primary tool for pitting mechanisms and a good one for general or area corrosion such as CUI.

From call-out to decision: the follow-up workflow

A GWT survey that stops at the report is only half done. A typical workflow, described qualitatively:

  1. Plan. The owner's inspector identifies lines and damage mechanisms to screen. The NDE provider reviews isometrics, coatings, insulation, supports and access, and proposes test locations.
  2. Collect. Collars are fitted at each location; data is collected in both directions with distance-amplitude reference from known features such as girth welds.
  3. Analyse. The analyst identifies welds, supports and fittings, then flags anomalous reflections and grades them by relative severity under the procedure.
  4. Report. Call-outs are reported with axial position, a severity category and confidence notes on range and coverage limits. Areas not screened (beyond bends, past flanges, out of range) are stated, not left blank.
  5. Follow up. The owner's inspector decides which call-outs to verify. Verification uses quantitative methods: UT thickness grids, corrosion mapping, profile radiography or PAUT, often after insulation or coating removal at that spot.
  6. Decide. Measured thickness feeds the API 570 calculations. If wall is below minimum, the owner decides on repair, replacement or an engineering assessment; Atlantis does not perform fitness-for-service assessments.
  7. Baseline and repeat. Where permanently installed collars or repeated surveys are used, comparing signals over time can improve sensitivity to change. The owner decides whether and when to repeat.

A frequent program weakness is call-outs that were never verified. If a screen produces a call-out and no follow-up is recorded, an auditor will reasonably ask what the owner knew and when.

Worked example, described qualitatively

A refinery has an insulated Class 2 hydrocarbon line running along a pipe rack, with history of CUI on neighbouring lines. Stripping the full run for visual and UT would mean scaffolding and weeks of insulation work. The owner's inspector asks for a GWT screen. The NDE provider sets test locations at intervals that account for two elbows and several clamped supports, removing a small window of insulation at each collar location.

The screen identifies welds and supports as expected, and three anomalous reflections between supports. Two are graded as minor and one as significant. The inspector directs insulation removal at all three for follow-up. Corrosion mapping at the significant call-out shows an area of wall loss under a damaged jacket seam; UT grids at the two minor call-outs show light surface corrosion. The measured data goes into the circuit's corrosion-rate and remaining-life calculations. The report also states which segments, beyond one elbow, were screened with reduced confidence, so the inspector can decide whether to add spot UT there. Intervals and repairs are the inspector's decisions.

Personnel qualification and procedures

Guided wave testing is recognized as its own method in ASNT's SNT-TC-1A, so employers can qualify and certify GW personnel under their written practice. Because interpretation depends heavily on the analyst's skill, owners commonly ask for the analyst's GW certification and for evidence of training on the specific equipment. A good procedure states the equipment, the wave modes and frequencies used, the pipe configurations covered, the reference method for amplitude, how call-outs are graded, how unscreened zones are reported, and how follow-up is recommended. The procedure should be reviewed by a Level III with GW and UT knowledge. For training under SNT-TC-1A, see ASNT Level III training.

What to include in a guided wave scope request

A clear scope makes the difference between a screen the inspector can act on and a report full of caveats. Before requesting GWT, owners usually assemble the following:

  • Line list and isometrics. Line numbers, sizes, schedules, materials and routing, with bends, fittings, branches and supports marked.
  • Condition information. Insulation type and jacketing, coating type (especially any bonded or heavy wrap), buried or cased sections, and known damage history.
  • Service conditions. Operating temperature at the collar locations, contents, and whether the line can stay in service during the survey.
  • Damage mechanism of concern. CUI, under-support corrosion, soil-side corrosion and so on, so the procedure and test spacing suit the target.
  • Follow-up expectations. Whether follow-up UT or corrosion mapping should be done in the same mobilization, and who authorises insulation removal at call-outs.
  • Reporting format. How call-outs should be referenced to isometrics or CML numbering so they can be traced in the owner's inspection records.

Doing screen and follow-up in one mobilization usually gives the inspector a decision-ready package; splitting them across months tends to leave call-outs unverified.

How Atlantis supports guided wave programs

Atlantis performs guided wave screening on piping and the quantitative follow-up that makes it useful: UT thickness grids, corrosion mapping, profile radiography by crews licensed where the work is done, and PAUT. Work is done by ASNT-certified technicians under ASNT Level III oversight, to written procedures that state coverage limits. We deliver results to the owner's API 570 inspector, who remains inspector of record and decides follow-up, intervals and repairs. Request a quote for GWT with follow-up; we respond within 24 hours.

Guided wave testing FAQ

What is guided wave testing (GW) in NDT?

It is an ultrasonic method that sends low-frequency waves along a pipe from a transducer ring at one point, detecting changes in cross-section over long distances. It is used as a screening tool.

Does guided wave testing measure wall thickness?

No. ASTM E2775 and E2929 describe it as screening that does not directly measure wall thickness. Follow-up with UT or other quantitative NDT is normally required.

What pipe sizes does guided wave testing cover?

The ASTM practices cover carbon and low-alloy steel pipe from NPS 2 to 48 with wall thickness from 0.15 to 1 inch, in a basic straight configuration.

Can guided wave testing inspect through insulation?

Yes. Only a small window of insulation is removed at each collar location, which is why it is widely used for CUI screening.

How far can guided waves travel in a pipe?

It depends heavily on conditions. Bends, coatings, soil contact, fittings and supports all shorten range. Expect much shorter range on coated or buried pipe than on clean pipe in air.

Can guided wave testing find pitting?

Small isolated pits are hard to detect because they change the cross-section very little. Use CML readings and scanning for pitting mechanisms.

Is guided wave testing accepted under API 570?

API 570 lets the owner choose inspection methods suited to the damage mechanisms. GWT is commonly used for screening within API 570 programs, with quantitative follow-up feeding the code's calculations.

Who is qualified to perform guided wave testing?

Personnel qualified and certified in the GW method under the employer's written practice, typically to ASNT SNT-TC-1A, with training on the specific equipment.

Planning a CUI or pipe-rack screen? Tell us about the lines or ask about road crossings and casings. Related: guided wave for pipeline inspection, NDE method selection by damage mechanism.
